headline: Decibel Q3 revenue rises 7% to C$35.1M as exports hit a record
dek: Decibel Cannabis reported on 19 November that international sales rose 44% to C$12.1M while Canadian sales fell 6%, and kept its 2026 guidance.
key_points: Net revenue for the quarter to 30 September was C$35.1 million, up 7% from a year earlier, with net income of C$3.8 million against a C$1.3 million loss.
International sales rose 44% to a record C$12.1 million; Canadian net sales fell 6% to C$23.0 million and market share slipped to 4.0%.
Gross margin before fair value adjustments widened to 52% from 47%, and adjusted EBITDA was C$7.4 million.
Decibel reaffirmed 2026 guidance of C$132 million to C$137 million in net revenue, which on our arithmetic implies C$31.4 million to C$36.4 million in the fourth quarter.
body: Decibel Cannabis is turning into an export business with a Canadian brand portfolio attached. The Calgary company reported third-quarter results on Thursday 19 November showing net revenue of C$35.1 million for the three months to 30 September, up 7% from a year earlier. All of the growth came from abroad. International sales rose 44% to a record C$12.1 million. Sales in Canada fell 6% to C$23.0 million. All figures are in Canadian dollars.

The company kept its full-year guidance of C$132 million to C$137 million in net revenue and C$28 million to C$32 million in adjusted EBITDA. It reported net income of C$3.8 million, or C$0.10 a share, against a net loss of C$1.3 million a year earlier. The release was reissued the same day with corrections; the figures here are from the corrected version.
## The export engine

This was the third record quarter in a row for international sales, which also rose 14% from the second quarter. Year-to-date international sales of C$32.3 million are already above the total for all of 2025 and are 92% higher than at the same point last year.

On our arithmetic, exports made up 34.5% of net revenue in the quarter, up from 25.5% a year earlier. The year-on-year growth rate has slowed from earlier quarters because AgMedica, the EU-GMP business in Chatham, Ontario that Decibel bought, was already in last year's third-quarter numbers.

Decibel says it has more than 20 international customers under signed supply agreements and more than 70 GACP cultivators and extractors supplying it. Its flower processing capacity is 60 tonnes a year and ran at about 42% in the quarter, which works out to roughly 25 tonnes a year at the current rate. The company says the Chatham site can double processing capacity without material capital spending, and that a backlog of orders remains to be converted into revenue.

The United Kingdom is the next launch. Decibel announced a deal with Hilltop Leaf during the quarter to bring its General Admission and Standard Issue flower to the UK across fifteen product lines, plus six Hilltop Leaf lines, in the fourth quarter. It has received a first order and is working towards a first shipment. StratCann reports that Decibel has exported to eight countries, including Germany, Australia, Israel and Switzerland. Management expects to enter three more markets within six months.
## The home market problem

Canada is where the pressure is. Chief executive Benjamin Sze said in the release that "we have work to do in our domestic business." The company put the 6% decline down to infused products shrinking as a share of the overall market, with lower General Admission sales partly offset by growth in Standard Issue.

Market share fell to 4.0% in the quarter from 4.3% in the second quarter, according to HiFyre data cited by the company. Decibel remains the fourth-largest licensed producer in pre-rolls, with 6.1% share, and in vapes, with 8.4%. General Admission is still the top infused pre-roll brand at 16.2%.

Excise tax explains part of the squeeze. StratCann calculates that Decibel paid C$13.4 million in excise on C$36.4 million of gross Canadian recreational sales, a rate of 37%. Derivative products such as vapes and infused pre-rolls are taxed by milligram of THC, which takes a bigger share of the price than the flat rate on flower. Decibel now plans to add flower and standard pre-rolls, categories it describes as long-standing gaps, and to focus on independent retailers.
> A third of Decibel's revenue now comes from outside Canada, where there is no 37% excise bill on the way out of the door.
## Margins up, cash thin

Gross margin before fair value adjustments rose to 52% from 47%, which the company credits mainly to better international margins. Adjusted EBITDA was C$7.4 million, up 2%. Adjusted net income fell 11% to C$3.3 million.

Cash generation is the weak line. Free cash flow was C$1.1 million in the quarter, down 31%. For the nine months it was negative C$8.7 million. The company puts that mainly down to a C$17.8 million rise in receivables and an C$8.3 million cut in payables, which it calls one-time and tied to its debt refinancing. Rising receivables are what fast export growth looks like on a balance sheet: product has shipped and the cash has yet to arrive. Whether those receivables convert is the figure to check in the annual results.
## What the guidance implies

Nine-month net revenue was C$100.6 million, up 20%, and nine-month adjusted EBITDA was C$22.2 million, up 30%. Set against the reaffirmed guidance, that leaves C$31.4 million to C$36.4 million of net revenue and C$5.8 million to C$9.8 million of adjusted EBITDA to come in the fourth quarter. Those ranges are our subtraction, not company figures. The low end would mean a quarter weaker than the one just reported. The top end would need exports to keep growing while Canada stabilises.
## A new shareholder on the register

The results arrived a day after Toronto investment firm Ewing Morris completed its offer for Decibel shares. As we reported on 19 November, it is paying C$2.09 a share for 2,230,198 shares, about 5.79% of the company, at a total cost of about C$4.66 million. StratCann reports that the board made no recommendation and that management did not tender its own shares. Sze told the outlet the company welcomes Ewing Morris as a shareholder.

Decibel also said it has started the steps needed to have a share buyback programme, known in Canada as a normal course issuer bid, available. The board does not expect material buying in the near term.
## What to watch

Watch the first UK shipment under the Hilltop Leaf deal in the fourth quarter and the three new export markets promised within six months. Watch Canadian market share after the 4.0% reading, and whether new flower and pre-roll products slow the decline. Watch receivables and free cash flow in the full-year results. And watch whether Ewing Morris, which describes its approach as active, seeks a role beyond holding the shares.
